The record:
Write the postmortem for the incident below.

Alert: FraudHoldsHigh on io-shop
What the alert said [AL1]: Share of purchases held for review above 10% {A1} for 5m {A2}
Alert raised: 2026-11-11T02:42:01Z {alert_raised}
Nobody was paged: no on-call incident was linked to this one. An alert rule fires; a person is paged. Argus first posted about the incident in Slack at 2026-11-11T02:42:25Z {first_told}, and the document says so already: leave that post out, and do not say that no person was told. That nobody was paged is a finding of its own.
The alert rule waits 5 minutes {rule_waits} with its condition holding before it fires. The alert came within the 7 minutes 30 seconds {accounted_for} accounted for by its rule waiting 5 minutes {rule_waits} with its condition holding, its evaluation at intervals of 1 minute {rule_evaluated_every}, an unmeasured allowance of 30 seconds {scraping_allowance} for scraping and storing its samples and the whole minute the onset is measured to.
Broken from 2026-11-11T02:35:00Z {began} (the onset) to 2026-11-11T02:43:00Z {back_to_normal}, when the metrics show it back to normal.
That is 8 minutes {duration}, and every impact figure below is measured over that stretch.
Argus held the incident for 2 minutes 41 seconds {held}, until 2026-11-11T02:45:03Z {argus_stopped}. That is not how long the fault lasted, nor how long Argus went on working - leave it out of your answer.
The service's error rate over all its requests, before it began: 1.1% {errors_before}.
The same rate while it was broken: 0.8% {errors_while_broken}, peaking at 1.5% {errors_at_worst} - no higher than the worst minutes of stretches as long before it began.
Rise above baseline: none - no more of the traffic failed while it was broken than before it began.
The series behind the alert, `avg(fraud_held_for_review_ratio)` - its alert said "Share of purchases held for review above 10% {A1} for 5m {A2}" - which its alert rule evaluates and calls worse rising: 4.7183333333333334% {series_before} before it began, 17.4625% {series_while_broken} on average while it was broken, and 18.85% {series_at_worst} at its worst. Say what it measures in words, not by its query.
No rise in failed requests was measured, so the harm to report is what this series did: say what it meant for the people using the service, not that little or nothing failed.
Customer loss: none - the shop's takings over the incident fell short of the same hours whole weeks earlier by no more than those hours vary on their own, if at all.

What Argus did, in order:
  - [T1] 2026-11-11T02:42:22Z {T1.1} Argus: Received FraudHoldsHigh on io-shop
  - [T2] 2026-11-11T02:42:27Z {T2.1} Argus: Moved the incident to INVESTIGATING - a worker took the incident up
  - [T3] 2026-11-11T02:42:27Z {T3.1} Argus: Called in the Investigator Agent
  - [T4] 2026-11-11T02:42:37Z {T4.1} Investigator Agent: Asked for the service's per-minute metrics, anchored on 02:42:01 {T4.2}
  - [T5] 2026-11-11T02:42:42Z {T5.1} Investigator Agent: Read back 360 {T5.2} minutes of metrics
  - [T6] 2026-11-11T02:42:43Z {T6.1} Investigator Agent: Placed the start of the incident at 02:35 {T6.2}
  - [T7] 2026-11-11T02:42:44Z {T7.1} Investigator Agent: Recorded where the service's replicas run - io-shop-7d9c4f8b6-m4q7r on Tesla-V100-SXM2-16GB, io-shop-7d9c4f8b6-c8v2n on Tesla-V100-SXM2-16GB. Started at the onset: io-shop-7d9c4f8b6-x2k9p on NVIDIA-A100-SXM4-40GB
  - [T8] 2026-11-11T02:42:45Z {T8.1} Investigator Agent: Asked for production change events - deploys, releases and flag changes on the service, the 1 {T8.2} day 1 {T8.3} minute before Nov 11 02:36 {T8.4}
  - [T9] 2026-11-11T02:42:46Z {T9.1} Investigator Agent: Read back 0 {T9.2} production changes
  - [T10] 2026-11-11T02:42:46Z {T10.1} Investigator Agent: Read how far the deployment had rolled out - all 3 {T10.2} replicas run one revision, which the history does not name
  - [T11] 2026-11-11T02:42:47Z {T11.1} Investigator Agent: Formed 1 {T11.2} candidate cause, best first: C1
  - [T12] 2026-11-11T02:42:47Z {T12.1} Investigator Agent: Did not read logs
  - [T13] 2026-11-11T02:42:47Z {T13.1} Argus: Read the flag provider's history - 0 {T13.2} flag changes by anyone but Argus, the 1 {T13.3} hour before 02:42:47 {T13.4}
  - [T14] 2026-11-11T02:42:52Z {T14.1} Argus: Moved the incident to MITIGATING to act on a candidate
  - [T15] 2026-11-11T02:42:52Z {T15.1} Argus: Called in the Mitigation Agent
  - [T16] 2026-11-11T02:42:54Z {T16.1} Mitigation Agent: Held the pods of io-shop to Tesla-V100-SXM2-16GB for C1
  - [T17] 2026-11-11T02:43:02Z {T17.1} Mitigation Agent: Waiting to see whether the service is still at the incident's level, from 02:43 {T17.2} - up to 185s {T17.3}
  - [T18] 2026-11-11T02:45:03Z {T18.1} Mitigation Agent: Looked at the service - no longer at the incident's level since 02:43 {T18.2}
  - [T19] 2026-11-11T02:45:03Z {T19.1} Mitigation Agent: Judged the action CONFIRMED
  - [T20] 2026-11-11T02:45:03Z {T20.1} Argus: Moved the incident to MITIGATED - held [io-shop]'s pods to [Tesla-V100-SXM2-16GB], where they had been held to no card and the rule that fired stopped firing
  - [T21] 2026-11-11T02:46:36Z {T21.1} Code-Fix Agent: Proposed a fix as a draft pull request - https://github.com/ohadraz/Argus-Demo-Target-App/pull/534

Changes to production it read:
  - Deploys read, none came back; flags read, none came back.

Log lines it read, one per message:
  - Not read.

Candidates it considered, in the Investigator's words - name them by their labels, but cite none; what they claim is not what happened unless a row of the record shows it:
  - [C1] At 2026-11-11T02:35:00Z {C1.1} the replica io-shop-7d9c4f8b6-x2k9p was placed on gpu-a100-0 (NVIDIA-A100-SXM4-40GB). The other replicas run on Tesla-V100 cards. The fraud-hold share rose from about 0.05 {C1.2} to 0.18 {C1.3} with nothing deployed. Errors, latency, memory and CPU stayed flat, so the fraud model is deciding differently on the new card. [accelerator-heterogeneity, confidence 0.82 {C1.4}, confirmed]

Actions it took:
  - [M1] Held the pods of io-shop to Tesla-V100-SXM2-16GB for [C1] (can be put back) - confirmed, still in place

What Code-Fix read in the source and proposed, in Code-Fix's words - nothing ran its test or its fix, and what it claims is not what happened unless a row of the record shows it:
  - [F1] The fault is in src/io_shop/fraud_scoring.py. The model's logit is the small difference between two products of about the same size and opposite sign (WEIGHT_ON_THE_CHARGE × charge and WEIGHT_ON_THE_SETTLEMENT × settlement, with the weights at 4680.05 {F1.1} and -4000.0 {F1.2}). `fraud_logit` passes every operand through `_to_tf32` when `runs_in_tf32(accelerator)` is true. That happens when `ALLOW_TF32` is True and the accelerator is in `TF32_ACCELERATORS`, which holds "NVIDIA-A100-SXM4-40GB". With only 11 {F1.3} significand bits kept, rounding the weights and features changes each product by more than the difference the decision depends on, so the logit on an A100 is mostly rounding error. Nothing in the code checks whether the model can tolerate that rounding. It turns on whenever the node happens to have an Ampere card, which is how one replica started holding many more purchases than its V100 peers without any deploy.
      
      The fix sets `ALLOW_TF32 = False` and says why in the comment: this model's opinion lives in a cancellation that TF32 destroys, so the speed-up costs correctness here. As a result `runs_in_tf32` returns False for every accelerator, and `fraud_logit` uses `_as_given` everywhere. That makes the score on an A100 the same as on a V100, and makes the scorer safe to land on any node. `TF32_ACCELERATORS`, `_to_tf32` and the function signatures are unchanged. The repository has no other callers of this module; the only reference is the test file.
      
      tests/io_shop/test_fraud_scoring.py adds three tests on "NVIDIA-A100-SXM4-40GB". The first checks that `runs_in_tf32` is false there. The second checks that `held_for_review` makes the same decision as on the V100 for every price from 500 {F1.4} to 8,999 {F1.5} pence. The third checks that fewer than 10% {F1.6} of those prices are held on the A100. Against the current code the A100 decisions are made with TF32-rounded operands, so the tests are written to fail there. With the change they should pass. I also updated the test file's docstring, which said Ampere behaviour was deliberately left untested.
  - Say what the files Code-Fix read do, with the conditions it gives - a default as a default, never as all it does - and no wider: 'nothing in the files it read', never 'nothing in the code'.

Action items the record already holds:
  - AI-1 (mitigate, done): Held the pods of io-shop to Tesla-V100-SXM2-16GB
  - AI-2 (prevent, open): Review and merge the proposed fix
  - AI-3 (mitigate, open): Turn automatic sync of io-shop back on once its repository says what should run - until then nothing merged reaches it, and turned on sooner it puts back what the repository says, undoing what Argus changed by hand
PR #534 is a draft Argus opened for a person to review and merge. The record holds nothing about it after that: do not say it was reviewed, approved or merged, or that it was not - nor that the record holds nothing, which the document says itself. Nothing ran its test or its fix: say what it proposes, not that it corrects anything.

Cite evidence in causal_chain by its label. In a contributing factor's addressed_by, name the record's own action items that answer it, by their number; an item you propose names the factors it answers in its answers, by their labels.

Call submit_postmortem with your answer.

The document, by field:
root_cause: The fraud model's logit is the small difference between two large products of opposite sign (weights of {F1.1} and {F1.2}). In src/io_shop/fraud_scoring.py, `fraud_logit` rounds every operand to TF32, which keeps only {F1.3} significand bits, whenever `ALLOW_TF32` is True and the card is listed in `TF32_ACCELERATORS`, and that list holds NVIDIA-A100-SXM4-40GB. On an A100 the rounding changes each product by more than the difference the decision depends on, so the logit there, and with it the hold decision, is mostly rounding error. It rests on F1, a reading of the source nothing ran, so it is unverified.
cause_in_plain_words: One copy of the shop's service started on a different kind of graphics card from the others, and on that card the fraud check likely rounds its numbers coarsely enough to change its decisions, so it held many more purchases for review.
still_at_risk: Any replica of the shop that lands on an A100 card again, once its pods are no longer held to V100 cards, could again hold far more purchases for review than its peers.
symptom: The shop held far more purchases for fraud review than usual
causal_chain 1: The shop held a much larger share of purchases for fraud review than before the onset, enough to fire FraudHoldsHigh. Failed requests did not rise. (cites AL1; T5, under "What Argus did, in order"; T6, under "What Argus did, in order")
causal_chain 2: As read at {T7.1}, the replica io-shop-7d9c4f8b6-x2k9p had started at the onset on an NVIDIA-A100-SXM4-40GB card. The other replicas ran on Tesla-V100-SXM2-16GB cards. (cites T7, under "What Argus did, in order")
causal_chain 3: Running the fraud scorer on the A100 card raised the share of purchases held. Once every pod was held to Tesla-V100-SXM2-16GB cards, the service was no longer at the incident's level from {T18.2}. (cites T16, under "What Argus did, in order"; T18, under "What Argus did, in order"; T19, under "What Argus did, in order")
causal_chain 4: On the A100 card, the scorer in the files Code-Fix read rounds the fraud model's weights and inputs to TF32, which changes its hold decisions. (cites F1, under "What Code-Fix read in the source and proposed, in Code-Fix's words - nothing ran its test or its fix")
contributing_factors 1: Before the incident, io-shop's pods were held to no card type, so the scheduler could put a replica on an A100 card next to replicas on V100 cards.
contributing_factors 1 had_it_been_otherwise: Had the pods been held to one card type, the replica started at the onset would not have landed on an A100 card, and the scorer would have kept making the same decisions on every replica.
contributing_factors 2: No check was seen that the fraud scorer makes the same decisions on every card type it can run on. The test file's docstring said Ampere behaviour was deliberately left untested.
contributing_factors 2 had_it_been_otherwise: A test comparing A100 decisions with V100 decisions would have shown the TF32 divergence before any replica scored real purchases on an A100.
action_items 1: Write the constraint holding io-shop's pods to Tesla-V100-SXM2-16GB cards into the service's repository, so that turning automatic sync back on keeps it rather than undoing it.
action_items 2: Add a check, run on every change to io-shop's scoring code, that compares the fraud scorer's decisions on each card type io-shop can be scheduled onto and fails on any disagreement.
action_items 3: Link the FraudHoldsHigh alert to an on-call rotation so that it pages a person when it fires.
went_wrong 1: The FraudHoldsHigh alert paged nobody: no on-call incident was linked to it.
got_lucky 1: Only the replica started at the onset landed on an A100 card. The others stayed on V100 cards, so the rise was confined to the purchases that one replica scored.

Not to be judged:
  - Names in braces, such as {T5.1} or {duration}, are figures code writes in from the row they name. They are not judged.
  - Action items propose what to do; they make no claim about the record.
  - Whether something went well, went wrong or was lucky is a judgement. Only a fact it states is judged.

Judge every claim in the document, and answer by calling judge_claims.

tools.description: Submit every claim in the document, each either as supported or as flagged. Supported: the document's own words, quoted exactly, and the record's rows that support it. Flagged: the document's own words, quoted exactly, why, and the record's rows that contradict it (none where no row speaks to it at all). Empty lists say the document makes no claim to judge.

why.description: One sentence: what the record holds instead. Never empty.

tools.name: judge_claims
